v1.1.0

Release Notes & App Version Display

Show the running version inside the app, compare it with the latest GitHub release, and render the release notes on a page — with GitHub as the only place a release is ever written. Publishing a release is the whole "changelog" workflow; the app just reads it.

Step 1: stamp the version at build time

The version is never typed into code. The release workflow passes the tag as a Docker build argument, and dotnet publish bakes it into the assembly's informational version. A local build with no argument falls back to a recognisable dev value.

API/Dockerfile (build stage) 
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
ARG VERSION=0.0.0-dev
WORKDIR /src
# ... restore + copy sources ...
RUN dotnet publish MyApp.API/MyApp.API.csproj -c Release -o /app/publish \
    --no-restore -p:Version=$VERSION

Step 2: read it back, one helper for every project

A small static class in the Shared project reads the version from the assembly and answers the three questions a UI needs: is this a dev build, how do I display it, and is a release newer than what's running. It deliberately compares only the numeric core, so v1.2.0, 1.2.0 and 1.2.0+abc123 are all the same version.

Shared/Common/AppVersion.cs 
public static class AppVersion
{
    public const string DevVersion = "0.0.0-dev";

    public static string Of(Assembly assembly)
    {
        string version = assembly.GetCustomAttribute<AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute>()?.InformationalVersion
            ?? assembly.GetName().Version?.ToString(3)
            ?? DevVersion;

        // strip the "+commit-sha" build metadata the SDK appends
        int metadata = version.IndexOf('+');
        return metadata >= 0 ? version[..metadata] : version;
    }

    public static bool IsDev(string? version) =>
        string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(version) || version.EndsWith("-dev", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

    public static string Display(string? version) =>
        IsDev(version) ? "dev build" : $"v{version!.TrimStart('v', 'V')}";

    // a dev build is never "behind" anything
    public static bool IsNewer(string? candidate, string? current)
    {
        if (IsDev(current)) return false;

        var candidateCore = Core(candidate);
        var currentCore = Core(current);
        return candidateCore is not null && currentCore is not null && candidateCore > currentCore;
    }

    private static Version? Core(string? version)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(version)) return null;

        string value = version.Trim().TrimStart('v', 'V');
        int suffix = value.IndexOfAny(['-', '+']);
        if (suffix >= 0) value = value[..suffix];

        return Version.TryParse(value, out var parsed)
            ? new Version(parsed.Major, parsed.Minor, Math.Max(parsed.Build, 0))
            : null;
    }
}

Step 3: the API proxies GitHub's releases

The frontend never talks to GitHub: the API fetches the releases, caches them, and returns them in the usual ApiResponse envelope. That keeps the optional access token on the server, avoids browser CORS and rate-limit problems, and means the page keeps working when GitHub is slow.

Infrastructure/Releases/GitHubReleaseService.cs 
public class GitHubReleaseService(HttpClient httpClient, ReleaseCache cache, IOptions<GitHubReleasesOptions> options)
    : IReleaseService
{
    public async Task<List<ReleaseDto>> GetReleasesAsync()
    {
        if (cache.TryGet(out var cached))
            return cached;

        try
        {
            var releases = await httpClient.GetFromJsonAsync<List<GitHubRelease>>(
                $"repos/{options.Value.Repository}/releases?per_page=30") ?? [];

            var result = releases
                .Where(r => !r.Draft)
                .Select(ToDto)
                .OrderByDescending(r => r.PublishedAt)
                .ToList();

            cache.Set(result, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(options.Value.CacheMinutes));
            return result;
        }
        catch (Exception exception) when (exception is HttpRequestException or JsonException or TaskCanceledException)
        {
            // GitHub down or rate-limited: an old answer beats an error page
            if (cache.Stale is { } stale)
                return stale;

            throw new HttpRequestException("The releases could not be loaded from GitHub right now.", exception);
        }
    }

    public async Task<ReleaseDto?> GetLatestReleaseAsync() =>
        (await GetReleasesAsync()).FirstOrDefault(r => !r.Prerelease);
}

The cache is the same locked-field idea as In-Memory Caching, with one addition — expired data isn't thrown away, it's kept as Stale so the failure path above can still serve it:

Infrastructure/Releases/ReleaseCache.cs 
public class ReleaseCache
{
    private readonly object _lock = new();
    private List<ReleaseDto>? _releases;
    private DateTime _expiresAt;

    public bool TryGet(out List<ReleaseDto> releases)
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            if (_releases is not null && DateTime.UtcNow < _expiresAt)
            {
                releases = _releases;
                return true;
            }

            releases = [];
            return false;
        }
    }

    // expired but still the best we have
    public List<ReleaseDto>? Stale { get { lock (_lock) return _releases; } }

    public void Set(List<ReleaseDto> releases, TimeSpan timeToLive)
    {
        lock (_lock)
        {
            _releases = releases;
            _expiresAt = DateTime.UtcNow.Add(timeToLive);
        }
    }
}

Configuration and registration

The repository to read is options-pattern configuration, validated at startup (see Strongly-Typed Configuration). A token is optional — it only raises GitHub's rate limit or unlocks a private repository.

Options + registration 
public class GitHubReleasesOptions
{
    public const string SectionName = "Releases";

    [Required]
    [RegularExpression(@"^[\w.-]+/[\w.-]+$", ErrorMessage = "Releases:Repository must look like owner/repository.")]
    public string Repository { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    public string? Token { get; set; }

    [Range(1, 1440)]
    public int CacheMinutes { get; set; } = 10;
}

services.AddOptions<GitHubReleasesOptions>()
    .Bind(configuration.GetSection(GitHubReleasesOptions.SectionName))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

services.AddSingleton<ReleaseCache>();
services.AddHttpClient<IReleaseService, GitHubReleaseService>((provider, client) =>
{
    var options = provider.GetRequiredService<IOptions<GitHubReleasesOptions>>().Value;

    client.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.github.com/");
    client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10);
    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd("MyApp");          // GitHub rejects requests without one
    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Accept.ParseAdd("application/vnd.github+json");

    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Token))
        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", options.Token);
});

The endpoints

The running version is public (a login screen can show it); the release list needs a signed-in employee. A 503 distinguishes "GitHub unreachable" from a real server fault.

API/Controllers/ReleasesController.cs 
[ApiController]
[Route("[controller]")]
public class ReleasesController(IReleaseService releaseService) : ControllerBase
{
    [Authorize(Roles = Permissions.Employees)]
    [HttpGet]
    public async Task<IActionResult> GetAllAsync()
    {
        try
        {
            return Ok(ApiResponse<List<ReleaseDto>>.Ok(await releaseService.GetReleasesAsync()));
        }
        catch (HttpRequestException exception)
        {
            return StatusCode(StatusCodes.Status503ServiceUnavailable,
                ApiResponse<List<ReleaseDto>>.Fail(exception.Message));
        }
    }

    [AllowAnonymous]
    [HttpGet("Version")]
    public IActionResult GetVersion() =>
        Ok(ApiResponse<string>.Ok(AppVersion.Of(typeof(ReleasesController).Assembly)));
}

Step 4: the page — badges and a tiny markdown renderer

The page compares the running version with the newest non-prerelease and shows Update available, Up to date or nothing for a dev build. Release notes are GitHub markdown, but the page only needs headings, bullet lists and paragraphs, so a 30-line parser that emits real Razor elements is enough — and because every line is rendered as text (never as raw HTML), a release body can't inject markup into the page.

Pages/ReleaseNotes.razor 
<div class="version-strip">
    <span>Running: @AppVersion.Display(runningVersion)</span>

    @if (latest is not null && !AppVersion.IsDev(runningVersion))
    {
        @if (AppVersion.IsNewer(latest.Version, runningVersion))
        {
            <span class="status-badge status-update">Update available</span>
        }
        else
        {
            <span class="status-badge status-ok">Up to date</span>
        }
    }
</div>

@foreach (var block in ParseNotes(release.Notes))
{
    @if (block.Kind == BlockKind.Heading)       { <h4>@block.Lines[0]</h4> }
    else if (block.Kind == BlockKind.List)      { <ul>@foreach (var line in block.Lines) { <li>@line</li> }</ul> }
    else                                        { <p>@string.Join(" ", block.Lines)</p> }
}

@code {
    private readonly string runningVersion = AppVersion.Of(typeof(Program).Assembly);
    private ReleaseDto? latest;

    private enum BlockKind { Heading, List, Paragraph }
    private record Block(BlockKind Kind, List<string> Lines);

    private static readonly Regex LinkPattern = new(@"\[([^\]]+)\]\([^)]+\)");

    // keep the link text, drop the markdown around it
    private static string Clean(string text) =>
        LinkPattern.Replace(text, "$1").Replace("**", "").Replace("`", "").Trim();

    private static List<Block> ParseNotes(string notes)
    {
        var blocks = new List<Block>();
        Block? current = null;

        foreach (var raw in notes.Replace("\r\n", "\n").Split('\n'))
        {
            var line = raw.Trim();

            if (line.Length == 0) { current = null; continue; }

            if (line.StartsWith('#'))
            {
                blocks.Add(new Block(BlockKind.Heading, [Clean(line.TrimStart('#'))]));
                current = null;
                continue;
            }

            if (line.StartsWith("- ") || line.StartsWith("* "))
            {
                if (current?.Kind != BlockKind.List)
                {
                    current = new Block(BlockKind.List, []);
                    blocks.Add(current);
                }
                current.Lines.Add(Clean(line[2..]));
                continue;
            }

            if (current?.Kind != BlockKind.Paragraph)
            {
                current = new Block(BlockKind.Paragraph, []);
                blocks.Add(current);
            }
            current.Lines.Add(Clean(line));
        }

        return blocks;
    }
}
Need full markdown (tables, code fences, images)? Swap ParseNotes for a markdown library such as Markdig and render its output — but then sanitise the HTML, because the release body is text someone else can edit.

Things to watch

  • The tag is the single source of truth. Release Pipeline strips the leading v from the tag and passes it as VERSION; if the tag isn't a valid version, Core() returns null and no "update available" badge is ever shown — safe, but silent.
  • Drafts and pre-releases. Drafts are filtered out; pre-releases are listed but never counted as "latest", so a beta tag doesn't prompt every user to update.
  • Cache duration is a trade-off. Ten minutes keeps you well inside GitHub's unauthenticated rate limit; lower it only together with a token.
  • Sits next to the docs-site version. This is the in-app counterpart of Versioned Releases & Auto-Deploy, which stamps the docs site's own version from package.json.
